Many families and schools have different ideas about how long children spend on screens, and this question matters greatly to young people. Some people care most about children's health and sleep, but other people in this debate mainly see devices as learning tools. After looking carefully at both sides, I believe that parents should limit screens but allow devices for learning.

The first view is mainly about the health of young children, which many people see as very important. We can explain how this works in a very simple way: long hours of screen time keep children awake late, so they sleep badly. A good example of this from real life is children who play games until midnight and feel tired in class. But we should remember that this view does not hold in every case, because a strict ban can make children feel left out.

The other group of people is more interested in the value of tablets for schoolwork. Their main argument is quite easy to follow and understand: apps explain a topic in many ways, so children learn at their own speed. People can see this clearly in daily life, for example in Thai schools that taught online during COVID-19. However, this side also has a weak point that we cannot ignore, because children often switch from a learning video to games.

In the end, there are good points on both sides of the debate on screen time. So, after I have thought about both views, my final answer is that a sensible limit is better than a total ban. I think this is the best answer for everyone because it keeps the benefits of technology and protects health.

Looking back at the arguments about sugar in school shops, I find one side clearly stronger. For these reasons, my answer is still clear: school shops should offer only healthy choices. This is the right choice, in my opinion, because school should help young people build healthy habits.

Many people have strong feelings about the time children spend watching television, because it changes daily life in both good and bad ways. It can bring real benefits such as learning about the wider world, but it can also cause serious harm such as less time for sleep and exercise. A real example of this that I know well is my younger cousin, who learned English words from cartoons. Of course, this advantage has its limits and does not apply in every situation, because many programmes for children are only for fun.

The picture is less positive when we turn to the biggest disadvantage, which is the loss of rest and active play. The reason for this harm is quite simple: hours in front of the screen replace play and sleep. This problem is clear in everyday life, for example in students who watch dramas late and feel sleepy in class. However, this disadvantage is not as hard to control as it first seems, because parents can set a daily limit and turn the television off at bedtime.

In the end, it is clear that children's viewing habits can bring both real benefits and real harm. When I put the two sides together, my answer is that the benefits outweigh the harm when viewing time is controlled. This seems the most sensible answer to me because children can learn from television and still stay healthy.

A real example that many people in Bangkok know very well is Siam Square, where tutoring schools stay busy at night. To be fair, however, this change also has a good side, because an experienced tutor can help a weak student catch up.

Looking back at both questions, I can now see after-school tutoring much more clearly. So, when I take everything together, my overall answer is that the trend is mostly negative. I feel sure about this view mainly because teenagers need time to rest, not only to study.

The growth of private tutoring for secondary school students is something many people have noticed, and it raises two questions. In short, this has happened mainly because of strong competition for places at good universities, and its biggest effect is the harm to students' sleep, health and free time. After thinking about both questions, I believe that private tutoring does more harm than good for most students.

To answer the first question, the biggest reason for this change is the race to enter a top university. The way this works is simple: every mark matters because the entrance exams decide which university a student can enter. Here in Thailand, this is clear to see in the months before the TCAS exams, when tutoring centres are full every weekend. But there is also a second reason that we should not forget: busy parents need a safe place for their children until they finish work.

On whether this change is good or bad, the most important point is the damage that long study hours do to teenagers. It is easy to see why this matters: students study at school all day and then again at night, so they sleep less. A real example that people in Bangkok know is Siam Square, where tutoring schools stay busy late into the evening. To be fair, however, there is also a good side, because an experienced tutor can help a weak student catch up in one hard subject.

Looking back at both questions, I can now see after-school tutoring more clearly. So, when I put everything together, my overall answer is that the trend is mostly negative for young people. I hold this view mainly because teenagers need time to rest and enjoy life, not only to study.
